lead: This unit explains how convolutional neural networks turn images into feature maps and then into decisions. It follows the path from one convolution to classic and deep architectures, transfer learning, visualization and detection. After it, the student can size a CNN layer, read a modern architecture, fine-tune a pretrained model and explain R-CNN, YOLO, segmentation and Siamese matching.
about: The unit builds a working picture of CNNs for image tasks. Chapter 3.1 starts with the convolution operation, kernels, padding and stride, so every later shape can be calculated. Chapter 3.2 adds pooling and non-linearities, and Chapter 3.3 assembles these parts into a basic CNN. Chapters 3.4 and 3.5 trace the move from AlexNet, ZFNet and VGG to Inception, ResNet and a short note on DenseNet. Chapter 3.6 shows how pretrained models are reused, Chapter 3.7 shows how learned filters and class maps are visualized. The last two chapters apply CNNs to object detection with R-CNN and YOLO, then to segmentation with FCN, SegNet, U-Net and Mask R-CNN, and to Siamese verification networks.

chapters.idea: Convolution slides a small kernel over an image and sums products to make a feature map that records where a pattern occurs.
chapters.depth: Define image tensor H×W×C, kernel K_h×K_w×C and bias. Use cross-correlation; libraries call it convolution. Output size H_out = floor((H + 2P − K)/S) + 1, with the same formula for width. Padding P adds a border; stride S is the step. Padding same keeps size when S = 1 and K is odd. Multi-channel input sums over channels; F filters give F output channels. Parameter count = K_h×K_w×C_in×C_out + C_out. Some syllabi call the kernel a filter or mask. Mention 1×1 convolution as a channel mixer.

figure.title: 3×3 kernel, stride 1, no padding
figure.aria: A 4 by 4 input grid with the top-left 3 by 3 window marked, a 3 by 3 edge kernel, and the 2 by 2 output grid.

chapters.example: Input I = [[1,2,3,0],[0,1,2,3],[3,2,1,0],[0,1,2,1]]; kernel K = [[1,0,-1],[1,0,-1],[1,0,-1]]; stride 1, no padding. Find the output size and the full output. Answer: H_out = floor((4 − 3)/1) + 1 = 2, so 2×2; output = [[-2,2],[-2,0]].
chapters.trap: Students forget the floor in H_out, add padding only once instead of 2P, or count one kernel depth instead of C_in.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: matrix multiplication and forward propagation; Unit 2: gradients for training.
chapters.leave: Backpropagation and optimizer details to Unit 2; full CNN training loop to 3.3.

chapters.idea: Pooling shrinks feature maps and keeps the strongest responses; non-linearities let the network learn curved boundaries.
chapters.depth: Max pooling takes the maximum in each window; average pooling takes the mean; global average pooling gives one value per channel. Pool size p and stride s; usual s = p and no padding. Output size uses the same formula with K = p and P = 0. ReLU f(x) = max(0,x) is standard after convolution; Leaky ReLU, sigmoid and tanh appear in older blocks. Pooling has no weights; max pooling sends gradient only to the maximum location. Some syllabi call pooling subsampling or downsampling.

figure.title: Max pooling 2×2 stride 2
figure.aria: A 4 by 4 input grid with the four window maxima marked, and the 2 by 2 max-pooled output.

chapters.example: Input 4×4 = [[1,3,2,4],[5,6,1,2],[0,2,7,1],[3,1,4,8]]. Max pool with 2×2 window and stride 2. Find the output. Answer: top-left max(1,3,5,6) = 6; top-right max(2,4,1,2) = 4; bottom-left max(0,2,3,1) = 3; bottom-right max(7,1,4,8) = 8; output = [[6,4],[3,8]].
chapters.trap: Pooling has no learnable weights, but window size and stride still change the shape; max pooling is not average pooling, and ReLU is not pooling.
chapters.leave: Activation derivatives to Unit 1; batch normalization to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A basic CNN stacks convolution, ReLU and pooling layers, then flattens into fully connected layers for classification.
chapters.depth: Use the block Conv → ReLU → Pool, repeated; then flatten, dense and softmax. Track shape and parameter count at every step. Convolution layers learn filters; pooling layers have no weights; dense layers combine features. A small CNN can classify 10 classes. Some syllabi call this the architecture of a CNN or a hands-on basic CNN. Keep the example small and exact.

figure.title: Basic CNN
figure.aria: A basic CNN pipeline from a 32 by 32 colour image through two convolution and pooling blocks to a 10-way softmax.

chapters.example: Input 32×32×3. Conv A: 16 filters of 3×3, pad 1, stride 1. Max pool 2×2 stride 2. Conv B: 32 filters of 3×3, pad 1. Max pool 2×2. Find the output shape after each block and the parameter count of Conv A. Answer: after Conv A 32×32×16; after pool 16×16×16; after Conv B 16×16×32; after pool 8×8×32; Conv A params = 3×3×3×16 + 16 = 448.
chapters.trap: Forgetting channels in parameter count and flatten size; padding 1 with 3×3 keeps H and W only when stride is 1.
chapters.leave: Training loop, optimizers and regularization to Unit 2; classic architectures to 3.4.

chapters.idea: Early ImageNet winners showed that deeper convolutional stacks with ReLU, dropout and small kernels beat hand-designed features.
chapters.depth: ImageNet classification uses 1000 classes. AlexNet: 5 conv + 3 fully connected layers, ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, max pooling, first kernel 11×11. ZFNet: tuned AlexNet with 7×7 first filters and stride 2; its visualization belongs to 3.7. VGG: repeated 3×3 convolutions with pad 1 and 2×2 pools; VGG16 has 13 conv + 3 fully connected layers. Compare design trends: deeper, smaller kernels, more parameters. Some syllabi call this evolution of CNN architectures.

figure.title: VGG first block
figure.aria: A 224 by 224 image passes through two 3 by 3 convolutions with 64 filters and a 2 by 2 pool to a 112 by 112 by 64 block output.

chapters.example: VGG16 input 224×224×3. First block: Conv 3×3 with 64 filters and pad 1; Conv 3×3 with 64 filters and pad 1; MaxPool 2×2 stride 2. Find the shape after the block and the parameter count of the first Conv. Answer: shape 112×112×64; first Conv params = 3×3×3×64 + 64 = 1792.
chapters.trap: VGG16 counts 16 weight layers, not 16 convolution layers; AlexNet starts with 11×11, ZFNet with 7×7, VGG with 3×3.
chapters.leave: Inception and ResNet to 3.5; training tricks to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Inception runs several kernel sizes in parallel; ResNet adds identity shortcuts so very deep networks can train.
chapters.depth: Inception or GoogLeNet module: 1×1 bottleneck, parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 and max pool branches, then concatenate. ResNet: residual block y = F(x) + x; bottleneck is 1×1, 3×3, 1×1; shortcut solves the degradation problem; ResNet-50, 101 and 152. Some syllabi list DenseNet; cover one short subsection: each layer connects to all later layers, so features are reused. Inception concatenates; ResNet adds.

figure.title: ResNet bottleneck
figure.aria: A ResNet bottleneck with 1 by 1, 3 by 3 and 1 by 1 convolutions plus an identity shortcut added to the output.

chapters.example: ResNet bottleneck: input 56×56×64; 1×1 conv to 16; 3×3 conv with 16 filters and pad 1; 1×1 conv to 64; identity shortcut. Find the output shape and total parameters of the three conv layers. Answer: output 56×56×64; parameters = (64×16 + 16) + (3×3×16×16 + 16) + (16×64 + 64) = 1040 + 2320 + 1088 = 4448.
chapters.trap: The shortcut adds tensors, so shapes must match; a 1×1 projection is needed when channels change. Inception concatenates, not adds.
chapters.leave: DenseNet detail only short; object detection to 3.8.

chapters.idea: Reuse a model trained on a large dataset, then adapt its learned features to a new task with less data and compute.
chapters.depth: Start from a model pretrained on ImageNet. Feature extraction freezes the convolution base and trains a new classifier head. Fine-tuning unfreezes some top blocks and uses a small learning rate; batch normalization layers often stay in evaluation mode. Small dataset: freeze more. Large dataset: unfreeze more. Match preprocessing: input size, mean and standard deviation. Some syllabi call this fine-tuning strategies; domain adaptation uses the same idea.

figure.title: Transfer learning
figure.aria: New images pass through a pretrained CNN and global pooling into a new 10-class fully connected layer.

chapters.example: ResNet-50 pretrained on 1000 classes; new task has 10 classes. The final feature after global average pooling has 2048 values. Replace the 1000-way FC with a 10-way FC. Find the number of parameters in the new FC and state a training plan for 2,000 images. Answer: 2048×10 + 10 = 20,490; freeze the conv base and train the new FC; if data is larger, unfreeze the last block with a small learning rate.
chapters.trap: Do not fine-tune all layers with a large learning rate; that destroys pretrained features. Replace the head and keep the same preprocessing.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 and 3.5 architectures; Unit 2 regularization and learning rate.
chapters.leave: Training from scratch to Unit 2; LLM fine-tuning to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Visualization opens the black box by showing which patterns filters detect and by inverting feature maps back to image space.
chapters.depth: Show first-layer kernels as edge and colour detectors. Deconvolution, also called transposed convolution or backprop-to-image, maps activations back to the input; Zeiler-Fergus deconv network is the classic method. Deep Dream does gradient ascent on an image to amplify features; repeated octaves create hallucination. Neural style transfer uses a content loss and a style loss; only a few universities teach its full math, so keep it brief. CAM and Grad-CAM weight feature maps by class evidence; Grad-CAM weights come from gradients of the class score.

figure.title: CNN visualization paths
figure.aria: Feature maps from a CNN go to a deconvolution path for reconstruction and to Grad-CAM for a class heat map.

chapters.example: A Grad-CAM has two 2×2 feature maps A1 = [[1,0],[0,1]] and A2 = [[0,2],[2,0]]. For class c the weights are α1 = 0.5 and α2 = 1.0. Compute the heat map ReLU(Σ α_k A_k). Answer: 0.5A1 + 1.0A2 = [[0.5,2],[2,0.5]]; ReLU keeps it unchanged.
chapters.trap: Deconvolution is not an exact inverse; Grad-CAM weights are gradients of the class score, not raw kernel weights; apply ReLU after the weighted sum.
chapters.leave: Full style transfer math only brief; generative models to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Detection finds both what and where: R-CNN uses region proposals plus CNN features; YOLO treats detection as one regression over a grid.
chapters.depth: Background: classification, localization and detection; bounding box (x,y,w,h); IoU = overlap area ÷ union area; non-maximum suppression; mAP. R-CNN: selective search gives about 2,000 proposals; warp each to 224×224; CNN; SVM; box regression. Fast R-CNN shares convolution features and uses ROI pooling. Faster R-CNN adds a region proposal network with anchors. YOLO: S×S grid, B boxes per cell, C class scores, one forward pass. SSD uses multiscale feature maps and default boxes. RetinaNet uses focal loss for class imbalance. Some syllabi call these two-stage and one-stage detectors.

figure.title: YOLO detection
figure.aria: An image goes through a CNN backbone into a 7 by 7 grid that predicts boxes and classes, then non-maximum suppression gives detections.

chapters.example: YOLO with grid 7×7, B = 2 boxes per cell and C = 20 classes. Each box has 5 numbers: x, y, w, h and confidence. Find the output tensor size and the number of box predictions. Answer: depth per cell = B×5 + C = 2×5 + 20 = 30; tensor = 7×7×30 = 1470 numbers; boxes = 7×7×2 = 98.
chapters.trap: YOLO predicts box coordinates relative to the cell, not absolute pixels; confidence is objectness, not class probability; NMS is not learned.
chapters.leave: Pixel masks to 3.9; full mAP derivation not needed.

chapters.idea: Segmentation labels every pixel; Siamese networks compare two inputs with shared weights to decide same or different.
chapters.depth: Semantic segmentation gives one class per pixel; instance segmentation separates objects. FCN: replace fully connected layers with convolutions, then upsample with deconvolution and skip connections. SegNet: encoder-decoder with pooling indices. U-Net: contracting path, expanding path and skip concatenation; common in medical images. Mask R-CNN: Faster R-CNN plus ROIAlign and a mask branch. Siamese: twin networks share weights and compare embeddings; contrastive loss, triplet loss L = max(0, d(a,p) − d(a,n) + α) and ranking loss. Only a few universities teach ranking loss in detail; give one line. Some syllabi call verification same/different matching.

figure.title: U-Net shape
figure.aria: A U-Net with an encoder, pool, upsample, skip concatenation and a 1 by 1 convolution to a 5-class mask.

chapters.example: U-Net input 128×128×3. Encoder Conv 3×3 with 64 filters and pad 1; pool 2×2; upsample 2×2; concatenate with the encoder skip; 1×1 conv to 5 classes. Find the final output shape and the channel count after concatenation. Answer: after encoder 128×128×64; after pool 64×64×64; after upsample 128×128×64; after concat 128×128×128; final output 128×128×5.
chapters.trap: Segmentation output has one label per pixel, not one per image; skip connections concatenate, not add; Siamese branches share weights.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 to 3.5, and 3.8 for Mask R-CNN; Unit 2 losses.
chapters.leave: Full medical applications not needed; generative segmentation to Unit 6.
